name: Gastric balloon / endoscopic sleeve

lead: An intragastric balloon is a deflated silicone balloon placed in the stomach, usually endoscopically, and filled to take up space and encourage fullness. It stays for months and is then removed. Endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG) is a separate procedure in which the stomach is sutured into a narrower tube without incisions.
Both are positioned between lifestyle change and surgery for people with obesity. They appear in hardmaxx discussions as a way to lose weight without a major operation.

paras: A balloon occupies stomach volume and slows emptying, which promotes early fullness. Research on gastric distension has shown that stretching the stomach activates satiety circuits in the brain and reduces food intake in lean and obese people. ESG uses sutures to reshape the stomach into a narrower tube.

Common effects are nausea, vomiting, cramps and reflux. Rarer problems include ulcer, perforation and obstruction after deflation or migration. The 2022 MERIT trial of ESG reported rare serious events such as bleeding and leak. Weight regain after balloon removal is common without behavior change.

lead: An intragastric balloon (gastric balloon) is an inflatable device placed in the stomach to help with weight loss when diet and exercise have not worked and surgery is not wanted or recommended. It takes up space in the stomach, which causes earlier fullness and slower gastric emptying [1]. Devices are usually filled with saline, and some contain a dye that colors urine if the balloon leaks [1].

Endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG) is a different, incisionless procedure in which a physician sutures the stomach into a narrower tube using an endoscopic suturing device. In July 2022 the US FDA authorized ESG with the Apollo Overstitch device for adults with BMI 30 to 50 [2].

Reported results are moderate: balloon studies cited by Wikipedia report roughly 11 to 14 percent total body weight loss for one swallowable balloon, depending on follow-up, and a 2022 randomized trial of ESG reported 13.6 percent total body weight loss at one year [1][2]. The procedures are marketed to people with obesity; in looksmaxxing forums they are mentioned as hardmaxx options, but the published research concerns medical obesity, not cosmetic outcomes.
infobox: About 4 to 12 months, depending on device [3]
Orbera, ReShape Dual Balloon, Obalon, Allurion Elipse, Spatz3 [1]
About $8,150; usually not covered by insurance [1]

paras: Wikipedia lists the main balloon systems: the ReShape Dual Balloon (two connected balloons), the single-balloon Orbera, which is typically placed for about six months, Obalon (one to three gas-filled balloons that are swallowed but need endoscopy for removal), the Allurion Elipse (swallowed, no endoscopy, passes naturally after about 16 weeks, CE-marked in Europe) and the adjustable Spatz3, approved for one year outside the US [1]. Grokipedia gives similar information on fill volumes of 400 to 900 mL and placement lasting 4 to 12 months [3].
ESG is not a balloon; it uses full-thickness sutures along the greater curvature of the stomach to narrow it, and is usually done with the Apollo Overstitch device [2].

Wikipedia notes eligibility under FDA guidance as BMI 30 to 40, or above 27 with weight-related comorbidity, and lists contraindications such as inflammatory bowel disease, delayed gastric emptying, pregnancy and warfarin use [1]. Grokipedia adds prior gastric surgery, large hiatal hernia and untreated psychiatric disorders, and describes use as a bridge before bariatric surgery in people with very high BMI [3].

The balloon occupies stomach volume and delays emptying [1]. Physiological studies show that stomach distension reduces food intake: in an older study a water-filled balloon reduced intake of a liquid meal in lean and obese subjects [4], brain imaging showed distension activates satiety circuitry [5], and combined distension and cholecystokinin reduced intake in humans [6].

A 2016 meta-analysis cited by Wikipedia found short-term weight loss and no deaths. In one Elipse study of 509 patients, average body weight loss was 13.9 percent at four months; pooled data from six studies showed 12.8 percent at 4 to 6 months and 10.9 percent at 12 months [1]. Grokipedia describes average total body weight loss of 6 to 15 percent and common regain after removal without ongoing behavior change [3].

For ESG, the 2022 MERIT randomized trial in 209 adults with BMI 30 to 40 found 13.6 percent total body weight loss at one year versus 0.8 percent with lifestyle alone; meta-analyses report about 16 percent, with limited long-term data [2].

Wikipedia lists nausea, vomiting, reflux, cramps and bloating as common with balloons, and esophagitis, ulcer and perforation as rare. Deflation and migration can cause bowel obstruction, and endoscopic placement has rarely been linked to death. The article cites an FDA letter to health providers on risks of liquid-filled balloons [1].

For ESG, Wikipedia cites GI symptoms in over 70 percent of patients (mostly resolving within about a week) and rare serious events such as hospitalization for pain or nausea (1.08 percent), bleeding (0.56 percent), leak or infected collection (0.48 percent), pulmonary embolism and perforation (each 0.06 percent) [2].

Wikipedia traces the idea to 1938 to 1939 reviews linking bezoars to weight loss, a 1979 self-experiment by A. Henning, and the 1985 FDA approval of the Garren-Edwards Bubble, withdrawn about seven years later because of complications. No new devices were approved until 2015, when the ReShape Dual Balloon and Orbera were cleared [1].
The first human ESG was performed in 2012 by Dr. Christopher Thompson, and the technique was later adapted to a full-thickness suturing device [2].

Controlled trials of ESG (the MERIT trial) and balloon studies report weight loss in people with obesity [1][2]. Registered trials include a 12-month adjustable balloon versus a 6-month fixed balloon [7], preoperative balloon use before gastric bypass in 314 patients [8], balloon effects on obstructive sleep apnea [9] and in adolescents [10]. Summary results for these registrations are not given here. No study has tested balloons or ESG for cosmetic or facial outcomes.

timeline.event: A. Henning uses a gastric balloon for obesity in a self-experiment [1].
Garren-Edwards Bubble becomes the first FDA-approved balloon; later withdrawn [1].
First human endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty performed [2].
FDA approves the ReShape Dual Balloon and Orbera [1].
